solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Good: this writer's allowed cocktail

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
this writer = I, the setter; 'this writer's' = I'M, I am

explanation.surface: Someone boasting that the setter is permitted a good cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter referring to themself, so it gives I, and the apostrophe-s supplies the rest of I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: A gimlet is a cocktail of gin and lime juice.

clue.text: One lake-fed river in land around Perugia

parts.note: the Tay is a Scottish river
L = lake, as on maps; it goes inside TAY

explanation.surface: A geography note about a lake-fed river in the countryside around Perugia.
explanation.walkthrough: Perugia is in central Italy, not far from Lake Trasimeno, which makes the lake-fed river sound like real geography.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by location: Perugia is the capital of Umbria, in central Italy, so the country around it is the answer.

clue.text: Distress in a damsel — chap to produce it?

indicators.note: to distress is to trouble or disorder, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: A melodrama: a damsel in distress, and a man who causes it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damsel in distress' is the stock phrase the surface leans on; here 'Distress' is the instruction and 'it' in the definition points back to the damsel's distress.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladies' man, a womaniser, is just the chap to leave a damsel distressed.

clue.text: Son in practice session raised game

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising the letters reads them bottom to top

parts.note: a net is a cricket practice session

explanation.surface: A son at practice who then takes up a game.
explanation.walkthrough: SINNET read upwards gives TENNIS. In cricket, nets are practice sessions in netted lanes, so a single session is a net.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by class: tennis is one of the racket games, and the practice-session surface points at its nets too.

clue.text: Spies sound sheepish stealing abstainer's bread

parts.note: the CIA, the US intelligence agency

indicators.note: the sheep's sound takes the abstainer's letters into itself

parts.note: TT = teetotal, an abstainer; it goes inside BAA

explanation.surface: Spies who sound sheepish after stealing a teetotaller's loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: TT, teetotal, is the usual crossword abstainer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: ciabatta is a flat, open-textured Italian loaf, so it is one kind of bread.

clue.text: Tory politician accepting trustee's case for cut to commuted offence

indicators.note: the politician takes the trustee's outer letters inside
a word's case is its outer letters
to commute is to change, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: first and last letters of TrusteE, placed between CON and MP

explanation.surface: A Tory politician taking a trustee's case to argue for a commuted sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal surface (trustee, case, commuted) is all misdirection: 'case' means outer letters and 'commuted' means rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: disobeying or disrespecting a court is itself a punishable offence, so the specific crime stands for the general word.

clue.text: First time out, savour chance to be star

indicators.note: points at the first letter of the word for savour
'out' as in knocked out or gone out: the letter that 'First time' points at leaves the word savour.

parts.note: TASTE (savour) with its first T (time) removed

explanation.surface: A debutant savouring the chance to become a star.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'first time out' is a debut; here it tells you T, time, is the first letter to go.
explanation.definitionFit: The typographical sense: the little star-shaped mark * is literally a star, from Greek asteriskos, small star.

clue.text: Struggled to be heard after Takada's final gong

indicators.note: takes the last letter of Takada
the word for struggled is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: warred = struggled; spoken it matches WARD

explanation.surface: A sports report: Takada struggled before taking a final medal.
explanation.walkthrough: The blocks are listed in answer order although A comes 'after' in the clue. A gong is British slang for a medal or honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A gong, in British slang, is a medal or award.

clue.text: House welcomes ambassador's meaningful work?

indicators.note: the house takes the ambassador in, as a host welcomes a guest

parts.note: Taurus is one of the twelve astrological houses
HE = His Excellency, an ambassador's title; 'ambassador's' = HE'S, placed inside TAURUS

explanation.surface: A grand house hosting an ambassador's important work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' looks like a building; it is a sign of the zodiac. The question mark flags the pun in 'meaningful': a thesaurus is full of meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesaurus is a reference work organised by meaning.

clue.text: Note parts tangled in disorganised angler's gear

indicators.note: the letters of 'tangled in' are put in a new order
the note splits the rearranged letters, sitting inside them

parts.note: N = note, the dictionary abbreviation; it goes between LANDI and GNET

explanation.surface: A fisherman's kit left tangled and disorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tangled' looks like the anagram indicator, but it is fodder; 'disorganised' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A landing net is the net an angler uses to lift a hooked fish from the water.

clue.text: Mirror and Times giving tip

parts.note: to mirror someone is to ape them

explanation.surface: Two British newspapers, the Mirror and the Times, passing on a tip.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mirror and the Times are both British national newspapers, which is the surface's disguise: here they are a verb and a sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the highest point or peak of something, as the apex of a triangle, is its tip.

clue.text: Point picked up by team where Magpies play

indicators.note: picked up as on a radio, so heard rather than seen

parts.note: a tine is a point, as on a fork

explanation.surface: A football report: a point picked up by the team at the Magpies' ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Magpies are Newcastle United, who play on Tyneside, the area along the River Tyne in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcastle United, nicknamed the Magpies, play at St James' Park on Tyneside.

clue.text: Once again phone engineers help put back line

parts.note: RE = Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

indicators.note: the word for help is placed backwards

explanation.surface: Engineers told to phone again to get a line back.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers (RE) are the usual crossword engineers; 'line' sits in the surface as a phone line.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dialling a number again is phoning 'once again', with the verb's RE- prefix doing the work of 'again'.

clue.text: Little bit close to Vanessa Bell

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

parts.note: Great Tom is a famous bell at Christ Church, Oxford

explanation.surface: Someone who sat near the painter Vanessa Bell, if only a little.
explanation.walkthrough: Vanessa Bell was a Bloomsbury painter, so the name reads as one person; split it, and 'close to' takes the last letter of Vanessa while Bell is a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom is a tiny bit, as in 'not an atom of truth'.

clue.text: Drink to Scottish having arrived unexpectedly

indicators.note: the Scots word holds the other inside it

parts.note: to blow in is to turn up unannounced; placed inside TAE

explanation.surface: A toast to a Scot who turned up out of the blue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink to' looks like a toast; 'to Scottish' means the Scots word for 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Table wine is ordinary wine drunk with meals.

clue.text: Permit what diners do during cheese course?

definitions.meaning: a permit here is an official document that lets its holder cross borders

definitions.text: what diners do during cheese course?
definitions.meaning: split the answer 4,4: the verb for handing on plus the fortified wine that goes round with the cheese

explanation.surface: A question about dinner-party etiquette at the cheese course.
explanation.walkthrough: At a formal British dinner the port decanter is passed round the table (to the left) with the cheese, so split the answer as PASS PORT.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a travel document permitting entry, and PASS PORT, what British diners traditionally do with the decanter over the cheese.

clue.text: Empire rebuilt by socialist first shown

indicators.note: built again, so the letters are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A fallen empire rebuilt by a socialist, and shown to the world.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as history; 'rebuilt' just rearranges EMPIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A film or play that premiered was first shown then.

clue.text: Theatre boxes always cheapest way to go?

indicators.note: the theatre encloses the other word, as a box encloses its contents

parts.note: e'er, the poetic contraction of ever; placed inside STAGE

explanation.surface: The theatre's boxes: always the cheapest seats?
explanation.walkthrough: Theatre boxes are the priciest seats, which is the joke; here 'boxes' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Steerage was the cheapest class of passage on a ship.

clue.text: A life story packing in sex appeal from page one?

indicators.note: the life story packs the other letters inside it

parts.note: used as itself, packed inside BIO
'it' is dated slang for sex appeal (the It girl); packed inside BIO after IN

explanation.surface: A racy biography that gets to the sex from the first page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Packing in' reads as a single phrase, but 'in' is fodder: BIO packs both IN and IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Ab initio is Latin for 'from the beginning', which page one is, for a book.

clue.text: Goidelic tongue repressed periodically

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter

explanation.surface: A Gaelic language that has been periodically suppressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Goidelic is the Gaelic branch of the Celtic languages, and the surface's repression of it is real history.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic of Scotland or Ireland, a Goidelic language.

clue.text: Person who can cure wind

definitions.meaning: a medical practitioner, one who heals the sick
the name for a cooling afternoon sea breeze in hot coastal places, such as the one at Fremantle in Western Australia

explanation.surface: Who can cure a bout of wind?
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'wind' as flatulence and the clue is a single question; it is a second definition, the breeze called a doctor in hot places such as Perth and Cape Town.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: the healer, and the local name for the cooling sea breezes of Perth (the Fremantle Doctor) and Cape Town.

clue.text: High-backed bench and light

definitions.meaning: a wooden bench with a tall back and arms, often with a chest under the seat
to light on something is to come down and rest on it, as a bird does on a branch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like a lamp or pale; it is the verb, as a bird lights on a branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: the old high-backed bench, and the verb for coming to rest, which light (as in alight) also means.

clue.text: In dentist, as terrified, have trying experience?

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words

explanation.surface: A terrified patient in the dentist's chair going through an ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: The dentist's chair makes 'trying experience' look like an ordeal; the question mark points to the other sense, trying as sampling.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste something is to try it, to experience it briefly.

clue.text: Slipping lead, police dog savaged old president

indicators.note: the first letter of the fodder is lost
savaged, torn about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: POLICE DOG without its first letter, P; anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A police dog that slipped its lead and savaged a former president.
explanation.walkthrough: The lead in the surface is a dog's leash; here it is the first letter of 'police'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Calvin Coolidge was the 30th US president, in office 1923 to 1929, so long enough ago to be old.

clue.text: Some gloomy youth became Home Secretary

parts.note: the initials of Home Secretary, the UK interior minister

explanation.surface: A gloomy youth who grew up to be Home Secretary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Secretary is the British government's interior minister; the surface imagines a teenage goth rising to the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Goths are young people of a gloomy, black-clad subculture.

clue.text: Passes days in Rome

definitions.meaning: passes as in passes away, a euphemism for stops living
in Rome means in Latin, the Romans' language; the Latin word for days is the same as the English verb

explanation.surface: Someone spending their days in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Rome' signals Latin rather than place: dies is the Latin plural of day.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: the euphemism passes (away), and the Latin plural of day, as in dies irae, day of wrath.

clue.text: Spoil no child, beginning to expect esteem

parts.note: someone who is not a child

indicators.note: takes the first letter of 'expect'

parts.note: to rate someone is to esteem them

explanation.surface: Parenting advice: don't spoil a child, start to expect respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoil no child' echoes 'spare the rod and spoil the child', which makes 'Spoil' look like part of the proverb rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To adulterate is to spoil something by adding inferior matter.

clue.text: Fierce combatant once stopped by macho guys

indicators.note: the veteran is plugged with the other word, like a stopper in a bottle

parts.note: a vet(eran) is a former combatant
he-men, placed inside VET between VE and T

explanation.surface: An old soldier stopped in his tracks by some tough guys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fierce combatant' reads as one phrase; the definition is 'Fierce' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Vehement means fierce or forceful, as in vehement opposition.

clue.text: Salad vegetable somewhat excellent?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a salad vegetable is rather good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat excellent' is read backwards: excellent gives RAD, then 'somewhat' adds ISH, just as 'radish' sounds like 'rad-ish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The radish is a peppery root eaten raw in salads.
